title: Becoming a teacher
hook: the Buddha sends his monks out to wander, and a stranger learns from the way one of them walks

segments.voice: Yesterday, your teachers: Sigala bowing to the directions, and the teacher who checks you understood. Your line was proud of you in public. Did you send that one sentence? Day one thousand twenty-nine.

A monk named Assaji is walking through the city of Rajagaha on his alms round, bowl in hand. He isn't preaching. He isn't saying anything at all. A young wanderer named Sariputta, a pupil of another teacher who is still searching for the deathless, sees him and stops. Something about the way this monk moves, going forward, looking back, eyes down, calm, makes Sariputta follow him down the street. When the round is done, he walks up and asks: who is your teacher, and what does he teach? Assaji answers that he's new, and can only say a little. A little turns out to be enough. The lesson started before a word was spoken.

That scene comes from the Vinaya, the book of the monastic discipline. A little earlier in the same book, there's another moment. The Buddha has a small group of monks who have understood the teaching, sixty, the text says, and he sends them out. Go and wander, he tells them, for the good of the many, for the happiness of the many, out of compassion for the world. And don't let two of you take the same road. Spread out. So teaching begins as walking. Not lecture halls. Roads, villages, alms rounds. And the Assaji story shows what that teaching could look like: a person whose way of moving made someone else curious. The Dhammapada puts the order plainly. In Max Muller's translation: "Let each man direct himself first to what is proper, then let him teach others; thus a wise man will not suffer." Yourself first, then others. The verse doesn't let the second step come before the first. This week has looked at teachers near and far, famous and forgotten. Today the arrow turns toward the listener. In this picture, nobody needs a title to teach. Someone who practices is often being watched by someone else: a child, a roommate, a coworker who notices how they handle a bad morning. Becoming a teacher, here, is less a decision than something that happens when practice shows.
screen: `GO AND WANDER, FOR THE GOOD OF THE MANY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like to try it: teach by example, starting with how you sit right now. Let the body settle, upright and easy, the way Assaji might have walked: not stiff, not showing off. Breathe. Then bring to mind one person who will see you today. Pick one small thing you'd want them to catch from you without being told. Patience in a line. Putting the phone down when they talk. A real thank-you to whoever serves your coffee. Don't plan a speech. Just let that one thing be the lesson. The bell holds the time.
Carika. The wandering the Buddha sent his monks on, so that the way they moved taught before they spoke. Today's words.
Your line: by example. Today, do your one small thing where someone can see it, and say nothing about it. Let it teach on its own. Day one thousand twenty-nine.

howItsDone: In Buddhist communities, monastics are expected to teach through conduct as well as words, and many lay Buddhists speak of practice at home and work as the way they pass the teaching on.

fork.setup: you're Assaji. a stranger stops you after your alms round and asks who your teacher is and what he teaches. you're new. what do you do?
options: say you're not qualified and walk on.
say you're new and can only say a little, then say it.
give a long sermon to impress him.
fork.reveal: Assaji admits he's new and gives a short answer. it's enough for Sariputta, who goes on to become a great disciple.

original.note: Pali carika: a wandering, a journey on foot; the word the Buddha uses when he sends the monks out.

trapdoor: what you thought: a teacher is someone who decides to teach.
what it means: in these texts, teaching begins with walking and with your own conduct, so the way you move can teach before you speak.
what a scholar hears: caratha bhikkhave cārikaṃ bahujanahitāya bahujanasukhāya, the sending out of the monks in Mahāvagga I.11, and Assaji's bearing in Mahāvagga I.23.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Mahavagga I.11 (sending out the monks)

notes: Editor: review updated to match the revised day 1028 (Sigala, not SN 45.2); the week recap by title cut, since day 1030 lays out the whole block the next day; 'anyone who practices is already being watched' softened to 'often'; 'tends to sound hollow' (narrator's verdict) replaced with a line about the verse's order.
Dhammapada 158 quoted from Max Müller (SBE 10, 1881); confirm exact wording and punctuation.
'Sixty, the text says': Mahavagga I.10–11 says there were sixty-one arahants in the world (the Buddha included); the script says sixty monks, matching the outline. Confirm.
Mahavagga I.11 paraphrased: 'go and wander for the good of the many ... let not two go the same way.' Rhys Davids & Oldenberg (SBE 13) wording not quoted because the writer was not certain of it.

Mahavagga I.23: Assaji's bearing ('going forward, looking back, eyes down') paraphrased; confirm. 'Goes on to become a great disciple' in the fork reveal is a general description of Sariputta; confirm.

The hook field is rewritten from the index hook ('the Buddha sent out the sixty; every practitioner teaches by example') to avoid the 'every' claim; the voice keeps the outline's idea as 'anyone who practices is already being watched by someone'.
Day 1029 is a week end; the teach looks back at days 1023–1029 by title.
'Teaching that skips the first step tends to sound hollow' and 'mostly isn't a decision' are the writer's framing; soften if needed.

Audit 2026-10-01: Sariputta was a pupil of the wanderer Sañjaya when he met Assaji (Mahavagga I.23), not teacherless: hook corrected. Garbled line "less a decision. It's what happens…" fixed. Fifth teach screen head (said before the fourth, breaking the order game) removed; four heads remain. howItsDone "often" softened to "many".
